steps.title: The NASHA Headquarters
steps.text: A cinematic, original 3D headquarters for a concept brewery-and-kitchen business. It is a static front end: no framework, no tracking, CSS 3D, SVG and a small raw-WebGL scene engine (the Living Headquarters), with a complete 2D fallback.

proof.text: The front end passes its browser suite on Chromium, WebKit and Firefox, with axe accessibility checks at three screen widths.

The Living Headquarters is tested on Chromium, WebKit and Firefox with WebGL (automated; physical Safari and iPhone are not tested): twelve structurally distinct agent worlds each with exhibits counted from recordings, a synthetic digital-twin district, a spatial hand-off network, research-institute stations and a nine-scene recruiter journey, with keyboard navigation, browser history, reduced motion, a forced no-WebGL fallback, axe checks and a tampered-recording refusal.
The business is a concept; no real company, customers or data are shown.

steps.title: Twelve agents, one city
steps.text: Twelve named agents live in four districts around a mission-control tower. 12 of them appear in recorded runs of real workflows (aegis, aethon, cortex, echon, nexora, novara, pyrix, quantix, synapse, vectra, veritas, zybrew); the others only appear in the invented schedule simulation.

proof.text: Counted from 36 recorded runs (2102 events, hash-chained and re-verified in your browser).
The invented week in Offline mode is labelled a simulation with invented tasks.

steps.title: A real governed workflow
steps.text: Inventory Crisis runs the lab's governed procurement workflow: evidence through THE WEIR, a proposal, a hold for human approval, an audited draft purchase order that can never be sent. Rule-based planner; no language model.

proof.text: 9 recorded runs including approval, rejection, retry and fail-safe paths; the draft table cannot hold any state but DRAFT_NOT_SENT.
2806 automated checks across 33 suites, 0 failed, 0 suites skipped (generated 2026-11-10T17:52:45Z, tests/run_all.py)

steps.title: Six missions, one orchestrated
steps.text: Six real missions run on the lab's components: A Inventory Crisis, B AI Quality Incident, C Customer Experience Recovery, D Brewery Production Planning, E Concept Menu Test Pack and F Demand Surge Response. F is an orchestrated workflow of eight dependent tasks: a fixed graph with retries, cancellation, a human approval hold and failure propagation. It is not autonomous delegation.

proof.text: Recordings per mission: A Inventory Crisis x9; B AI Quality Incident x7; mission-c-customer-recovery x5; D Brewery Production Planning x5; mission-e-chef-test-pack x5; mission-f-demand-surge-response x5. Each is replayed after its hash chain verifies in the browser.
Every mission ends in a draft or a refusal. Nothing is sent, ordered, published or paid; the approval gate is exercised in the recordings, including rejection and expiry.

steps.title: AI evaluation and reliability
steps.text: AI Quality Incident checks a drafted answer claim by claim against the lab's status-aware knowledge base, applies five written criteria, blocks the release, and leaves a person to approve a corrected draft. Mission B now also runs the improved claim checker as a second opinion that can only downgrade a claim. The response under review is a scripted fixture.

proof.text: The Governance Fortress ran 19 of 19 bounded scenarios against the real components, and each scenario is shown to fail when its control is removed.
Customer-feedback classifier: sentiment accuracy 0.938, issue recall 1.0, measured on synthetic text written by the same author as the rules; real-world accuracy is unknown.

Own evaluation (claim-grounding-v1, 20 author-written items): the Mission B checker did NOT meet its acceptance criteria (false-support rate 0.3333); both negative controls fail, so the harness is sound. Language-model result: see the Research Laboratory (a real local model was run in Phase 7; it did not meet the thresholds).

Evaluation outcomes are shown as they ended, not as successes: the live model evaluation has not met its acceptance criteria (failed), and the remaining evaluation and cloud work is unfinished or not approved.

steps.title: AI Research Laboratory
steps.text: Six stations over stored results: claim verification (the four historical false acceptances stay visible), RAG investigation of the real knowledge base with visible abstention, agent reliability over every recording, model comparison, a regression laboratory and an evidence vault with four labels.

proof.text: The original claim checker accepted 4 unsupported claims on the historical benchmark (false-acceptance rate 0.3333) and false-acceptance rate 0.4091 on a separately written holdout. The remediated checker scores 0.0 on the holdout with 20% of true claims sent to a person.
Limits stated in the lab: labels are author-written (same author as the checker), the datasets are small and about one synthetic corpus, so this is not independent validation.

REAL local inference (qwen2.5:1.5b-instruct, digest 65ec06548149, ollama 0.40.15, loopback only) on all 57 items: with the unchanged prompt the model declared 0 claims SUPPORTED (it behaves like an always-UNSUPPORTED control; holdout accuracy 0.5946 against 0.9189 for the improved deterministic checker). A second prompt tuned on the development set reached holdout false-acceptance 0.3636. Neither meets the pre-registered thresholds; only the deterministic checker does.

Model-assisted Mission F (experimental): with the revised prompt the model produced a valid plan in 10 of 10 requests, but 10 of 10 valid plans were identical to the fixed graph, so no benefit is shown; only 5 of 10 explanations passed grounding. Every output is validated, the fixed graph is the fallback, and a person approves. The prompts were revised on the same requests, so this is a development-set measure.

steps.title: Business analytics and automation
steps.text: One synthetic dataset from the lab's warehouse feeds eight departments. Change a stock level, demand, a supplier price or a brewery outage and see availability, procurement, cost, guest feedback and marketing respond. Customer Experience Recovery joins synthetic feedback to the same warehouse.

proof.text: The twin's baseline reorder and negative-feedback share equal what the recorded missions produced; its JavaScript matches a Python reference on golden vectors.
NASHA is a concept; this is a simulation of a business that does not exist. Not a forecast.

steps.title: The technical architecture
steps.text: An optional WebGL prototype exists as an isolated experiment; the CSS 3D Agent City remains the supported view. Seven separated layers: a cinematic front end; an event-driven presentation layer that is a pure function of nasha.event.v1 events; backend orchestration; agent and analytical capabilities; governance and approval; evaluation and observability; synthetic business data. Standard-library Python, server-sent events, SHA-256 hash chains, loopback-only and token-protected.

proof.text: The event contract is versioned, schema-validated on both ends, and replay is deterministic.

Not built: a language-model planner that adds value over the fixed graph (the experimental one validates but does not improve it), multi-user identity, a trusted-network deployment for phones, and independent evaluation by someone other than the author.
